summary: This informational memo records experience building and using NeTraMet, a traffic meter, and NeMaC, a manager and meter reader, based on the Traffic Flow Measurement architecture. It offers guidance on writing rule sets and setting up a measurement system.

eli5.summary: Lessons from setting up counters on a road to learn which kinds of cars use it and how often.

questions: how to measure network traffic flows
how does netramet measure network traffic
how to implement a traffic meter
subtitle: Practical lessons from building and using the NeTraMet traffic measurement system.

tldr.problem: Organizations need to measure network traffic flows to understand usage patterns, bill users, and diagnose problems, but implementing a scalable measurement system requires careful choices about hardware, data structures, and packet matching algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: NeTraMet is a traffic meter that runs on modest PC or Unix hardware, uses a rule-based packet matching engine to classify flows, stores flow data in memory with efficient hashing and garbage collection, and provides SNMP access for managers to configure it and collect results.
tldr.outcome: Organizations from Australia to Europe successfully deployed NeTraMet for usage-based billing and network planning. The document captures three years of implementation experience and provides practical guidance on rule set writing, data collection, and system setup.

today: RFC 2123 documents NeTraMet as it existed in early 1996—a mature, production-quality system. NeTraMet influenced the development of IETF standards for traffic measurement (RFC 2063 and 2064). Modern network traffic measurement often uses software-defined networking, NetFlow, and sFlow rather than packet-matching rules, but NeTraMet's core ideas—efficient flow classification, memory-conscious storage, and SNMP-based management—remain relevant. The implementation lessons about hash tables, garbage collection, and rule optimization apply to any packet processing system.

sections.title: From Theory to Practice
sections.content:
In 1992, the Internet Accounting Working Group defined a Traffic Flow Measurement Architecture for standardizing how networks measure traffic. Nevil Brownlee at the University of Auckland took on the challenge of implementing this architecture. After developing a prototype using balanced binary trees (which proved too slow), he created NeTraMet, released as free software in October 1993. The system includes:

  • NeTraMet: the traffic meter itself, which observes packets and classifies them into flows
  • NeMaC: a combined manager and meter reader that downloads rule sets to meters and collects measured flow data
  • Analysis applications: tools like fd_filter (to compute data rates) and nifty (an X/Motif real-time flow viewer)

By early 1996, NeTraMet was in production use at many sites worldwide, with an active mailing list of about 130 subscribers. The system has proven particularly valuable for Internet Service Providers (ISPs) in Australia and New Zealand, and for networks like the Kawaihiko network connecting New Zealand universities.
sections.eli5: A university needed to count traffic, built a program to do it, and released it for free; now many networks use it to measure what their users are doing.

sections.title: Implementation Choices
sections.content:
Brownlee's first key decision was platform. Rather than use expensive Unix servers, he implemented NeTraMet on a DOS PC. This choice forced the implementation to be efficient (if it works on a 10 MHz 286, it works anywhere) and affordable (sites could deploy many meters). The meter platform provides Ethernet packet capture, system timing better than 10ms, IP for communicating with managers, and SNMP for the Meter MIB.

For packet capture on DOS, he used the CRYNWR Packet Drivers (available for many cards) to access promiscuous mode. For timing, he bypassed DOS's slow BIOS timer by directly reading the hardware timer, achieving 5ms resolution. He chose Waterloo TCP (public domain) for IP stack and CMU SNMP for the SNMP agent.

Data structures are critical: flow data is stored in fixed-size C structures, indexed by a large hash table. Rules are also C structures, organized into rule sets. NeTraMet uses a Packet Matching Engine that extracts attribute values (protocol, addresses, ports) from each packet and tests them against rules in sequence.

To optimize performance, Brownlee implemented several techniques: hash-based group testing converts large sequences of rules testing one attribute to hashed lookups (essential for 'test if source IP is in this list of 100 networks'); compressed address masks stores mask values in a table, reducing per-flow memory; and selective packet processing ignores protocols the rule set doesn't care about, avoiding wasted processing on, say, Novell packets when only IP flows matter.
sections.eli5: The program runs on cheap PCs so it's efficient, uses clever data structures to count millions of flows without running out of memory, and skips work on traffic it doesn't need to measure.

sections.title: Meter Management and Memory
sections.content:
NeTraMet stores flow records in memory and must recover memory from old flows. An incremental garbage collector periodically scans the flow table, removing flows that have been idle (no packets) and have been read by all known meter readers. To handle multiple meter readers collecting asynchronously, the meter tracks a collectors table recording the start time of each reader's last two collections; flows idle since the second-to-last collection can be freed.

To prevent memory exhaustion, NeTraMet monitors the active flow percentage. If it exceeds a HighWaterMark (typically 65%), the meter switches to a standby rule set that collects less detailed information, giving garbage collection a chance to free memory. If the percentage reaches a FloodMark (typically 95%), the meter switches to a minimal default rule set. This strategy has allowed the University of Auckland's meter to continue running for days after a meter reader failure, accumulating flow data until collection resumed.

NeTraMet collects data when a meter reader issues an SNMP SET request, setting a LastTime variable to mark the start of a collection. The reader then retrieves flows using SNMP GETNEXT requests on a TimeFilter window in the flow table, minimizing the SNMP overhead. For large flow volumes, NeTraMet returns column activity data as SNMP Opaque objects (raw binary blocks containing flow number plus data value), dramatically reducing SNMP packet count compared to reading individual variables.
sections.eli5: The meter keeps old flow counts until managers read them, automatically forgets data it doesn't need, and can run in low-detail mode if it's getting overwhelmed, like a bouncer letting fewer people dance if the floor gets too crowded.

sections.title: Writing Rules to Classify Flows
sections.content:
A rule set specifies which packets to count and what attributes to extract from them. NeMaC reads rule sets from text files, each containing a SET number, a RULES section, and a FORMAT section specifying which flow attributes to collect.

Each rule tests a packet attribute (e.g., SourcePeerType) against a value using a mask (e.g., 'is IP?'), and specifies an action: Ignore, CountPkt, PushPkt (record an attribute), Goto (jump to another rule), or Fail/NoMatch (retry packet matching in the reverse direction). Subroutines are supported via GoSub and Return actions, and meter variables (V1–V5) allow reusable subroutine logic. Computed attributes like FlowClass can be set by rules to tag flows with metadata for later analysis.

Practical examples include a simple rule set that records all flows on a network segment (pushing all Peer and Transport addresses) and a complex one that classifies traffic between gateways. The Kawaihiko example demonstrates a 650-rule set that classifies flows based on whether their endpoints are in the Kawaihiko network, other New Zealand networks, or international networks. Rules are arranged by subnet size (testing most specific masks first) so any IP address is classified with only nine comparisons, despite about 600 networks being tested.
sections.eli5: Rules are like instructions: 'if this is an IP packet, record the source and destination addresses; if one end is a well-known port, note which one.' Complex rules can ask 'is this IP address one of these 100 networks?' by using a clever lookup table.

sections.title: Building and Running a Measurement System
sections.content:
Setting up a NeTraMet measurement system requires several steps. First, decide what to measure: specify exactly which flows are of interest and what reports will be generated. This determines where meters are placed and whether PCs will suffice.

Second, develop a rule set and a standby rule set (a low-detail fallback). A common approach starts with the meter's default rule set to observe protocol distribution, then gradually increases granularity (e.g., adding Transport address matching to differentiate DNS from web traffic).

Third, configure meter readers. NeMaC can manage multiple meters simultaneously, each with its own rule set and collection interval. A keepalive mechanism detects meter restarts (by checking sysUptime) and automatically redownloads rule sets.

Fourth, develop analysis applications to process collected flow data and generate reports. The Kawaihiko network uses a 650-rule set to classify flows, then generates weekly traffic plots and traffic matrices showing average, quartile, and maximum rates between all pairs of sites.

Performance is good: a 10 MHz 286 handles 750 pps, a 25 MHz 386SX handles 1250 pps, and a 40 MHz 486 handles peaks of 3000 pps. The Unix version running on a SPARC 10 uses only 1% CPU while metering an FDDI interface.
sections.eli5: You plan what to count, write the counting rules, set up the computer, and decide how often to collect the results and what reports to make from them.
